facts.quote: The multi-week period following the end of each quarter when most public companies release their earnings reports is known as earnings season.
facts.claim: Earnings season is the few weeks after each quarter ends, when most public companies report.

facts.quote: It typically begins the first two weeks after the end of each quarter (namely early/mid-January, early/mid-April, early/mid-July and early/mid-October).
facts.claim: Earnings season usually starts in early to mid January, April, July and October.

facts.quote: Since the majority of public companies use calendar quarters (the end of March, June, September and December), earnings season focuses on this schedule.
facts.claim: Most companies use calendar quarters, so the season follows the March, June, September and December quarter ends.

facts.quote: Some companies deviate from the standard calendar, generally due to seasonal factors in the operation of their business.
facts.claim: Some companies run on their own fiscal calendar, so they report outside the usual weeks.

facts.quote: For example, retailers might end the quarter in January instead of December to account for winter holidays and other seasonal sales and returns during the same quarter.
facts.claim: A retailer may end its quarter in January rather than December, so its report comes on a different schedule.

facts.quote: But companies are free to announce their results before they officially file the required forms, and most do so, resulting in earnings season commencing well before the deadline.
facts.claim: Companies choose their own report date, and most report well before the SEC filing deadline.

facts.quote: Companies usually release their earnings reports and accompanying press releases before the market opens or after it closes.
facts.claim: Most companies release earnings before the open or after the close, not during regular trading.

facts.quote: If a company does issue a press release, it’s required to file an SEC Form 8-K, which must include the text of the release.
facts.claim: A company that issues an earnings press release must file it with the SEC on a Form 8-K.

facts.quote: A company beats (exceeds) the estimate or misses (falls short of) the estimate based on how actual earnings or revenues compare to the consensus.
facts.claim: A beat means actual earnings or revenue came in above the consensus estimate; a miss means below it.

facts.quote: several groups track a “consensus” estimate that’s the average for all the analysts covering the stock.
facts.claim: The consensus is the average estimate of the analysts who cover the stock.

facts.quote: This whisper number can become the market expectation rather than the official estimate.
facts.claim: The market's real expectation can be an unofficial 'whisper number', not the posted consensus.

facts.quote: But simply beating or missing estimates isn’t always what moves a company’s stock price.
facts.claim: A beat or a miss alone does not decide which way the stock moves.

facts.quote: Sometimes a company might beat estimates but provide a dour outlook for the future, leading the share price to drop.
facts.claim: A company can beat estimates and still fall if its outlook disappoints.

facts.quote: Other times a stock that rallied ahead of its earnings release and met expectations by reporting great numbers simply doesn’t have enough new buyers to bid the shares higher, causing share prices to hold steady or perhaps fall.
facts.claim: A stock that ran up into its report and met expectations can stall or fall for lack of new buyers.

facts.quote: Earnings season can be a busy and volatile time in the stock market.
facts.claim: Earnings season is busy and volatile.

facts.quote: you can find all of a company’s past earnings statements, as well as other important regulatory disclosures, free of charge on the SEC’s EDGAR website
facts.claim: Past earnings statements and other filings are free on the SEC's EDGAR website.

facts.quote: Regular trading hours for stocks traded on exchanges and certain other markets are from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
facts.claim: The regular session runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

facts.quote: Companies may announce important news or financial information outside of regular trading hours. These announcements, combined with other extended-hours trading risks, may lead to significant price changes in these companies’ stocks during extended hours trading.
facts.claim: News released outside regular hours can move the stock sharply in extended-hours trading.

facts.quote: The prices of some stocks traded during extended-hours trading may not reflect the prices of those stocks during regular hours, either at the end of the regular trading session or upon the opening of regular trading the next business day.
facts.claim: An after-hours price may not match the next morning's opening price.

facts.quote: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order. The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: A stop price is a trigger: once hit, the stop becomes a market order with no promised price.

facts.quote: The execution price an investor receives for this market order can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the prices of available liquidity when the market order executes.
facts.claim: A triggered stop can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: An investor can avoid the risk of a stop order executing at an unexpected price by placing a stop-limit order, but the limit price may prevent the order from being executed.
facts.claim: A stop-limit order avoids a bad fill but may not fill at all.

facts.quote: The report must be filed for each of the first three fiscal quarters of the company's fiscal year.
facts.claim: A company files a quarterly report (10-Q) for each of its first three fiscal quarters.

facts.quote: Key: Pre-Market After Hours Time Not Supplied
facts.claim: Nasdaq's earnings calendar marks each report as pre-market, after hours, or time not supplied.

facts.claim: Between sessions, the next chance to trade at market is the next open, which can be far from the prior close.

facts.claim: Earnings released between sessions are one of the things that move a price overnight.

facts.quote: A price gap occurs when a stock's price makes a sharp move up or down with no trading occurring in between. It can happen because of factors like earnings announcements, a change in an analyst's outlook, or a news release.
facts.claim: A gap is a sharp move with no trading in between, and earnings are a common cause.

facts.quote: Gaps frequently occur when exchanges open or when news or events outside of trading hours have created an imbalance in supply and demand.
facts.claim: Gaps often show up at the open after news outside trading hours.

facts.quote: The chart below shows a stock that "gapped down" from more than $34 to around $32 between a previous closing price and the next opening price.
facts.claim: Schwab's example: a stock gaps from above $34 at the close to about $32 at the next open.

facts.claim: In that example a $34 sell stop triggers at the open and sells at $32.

facts.quote: when the stock gaps down in the morning (lower than the prior day's closing price), your execution price could be significantly lower than your stop price.
facts.claim: After a gap down at the open, a sell stop can fill well below its stop price.

facts.quote: Generally does not work well in halted or gapping markets
facts.claim: Schwab rates stop orders as generally not working well in gapping markets.

facts.claim: The priced move for an event is not a promised size and says nothing about direction.

facts.quote: This tells the trader the options market has priced in a $10 move, whether as low as $90 or as high as $110, due to an upcoming event like earnings.
facts.claim: A priced move of plus or minus $10 on a $100 stock covers a range from $90 to $110 for an event like earnings.

facts.quote: Of course, there are no guarantees. The actual move could be more or less, up or down, or there could be no reaction at all.
facts.claim: The actual move can be bigger or smaller than the priced move, either way, or nothing at all.

facts.quote: Checking the MMM on an existing position ahead of earnings might be a good way to decide if it's worth the risk to hold through the event.
facts.claim: Checking the priced move before earnings helps you decide whether holding through is worth the risk.

facts.quote: Whether or not to hold in this situation depends on the trader's overall risk tolerance.
facts.claim: Whether to hold through depends on how much risk you can take.

facts.quote: When the market is pricing in a potentially outsized move, such as right before an earnings release or other company announcement, front-month IV might be higher.
facts.claim: Right before earnings, near-term option volatility can be higher because a big move is priced in.

facts.quote: in an attempt to capitalize on the expected collapse of IV that can often come after the market's initial reaction to earnings releases.
facts.claim: Option volatility often collapses after the first reaction to an earnings release.

facts.quote: The image above shows a stock trading at $216.88 with an MMM of ±16.74. This indicates the options market has priced in a move to as low as $200.14 and as high as $233.62.
facts.claim: Schwab's example: a $216.88 stock with a priced move of $16.74 either way.

facts.quote: Every quarter, hundreds of companies report earnings results within a compressed window, and the market's reaction can be swift and significant.
facts.claim: Each quarter hundreds of companies report in a short window, and reactions can be fast and large.

facts.quote: For traders holding stock, that means binary outcomes with full exposure to a potential move in either direction.
facts.claim: Holding shares into a report exposes you fully to a move either way.

facts.quote: Holding stock into earnings is straightforward but blunt. There is no way to limit downside without exiting the position.
facts.claim: With shares alone, the only sure way to cap your earnings risk is to be out of the position.

facts.quote: This last point is particularly relevant around earnings, where implied volatility is typically elevated. The market prices in an expected move
facts.claim: Around earnings, option prices carry an expected move for the report.

facts.quote: A stock is trading at $200 ahead of earnings and the options market is implying a move of around 8% in either direction.
facts.claim: Cboe's example: a $200 stock with options implying about 8% either way.

facts.quote: Single stock options heading into earnings often carry high implied volatility, which inflates the premium on both calls and puts.
facts.claim: Stock options going into earnings usually carry high implied volatility.

facts.quote: Options markets signal the market’s expectation for the stock’s move after the earnings release. The simplest way to see that anticipated move is to look at the nearest term, at-money straddle.
facts.claim: The nearest at-the-money straddle shows the move the options market expects from the report.

facts.quote: This could result in a stop loss order being executed at a price that is dramatically different than what your stop loss price indicates.
facts.claim: Company news can make a stop loss fill far from its stop price.

facts.quote: Earnings reports can move a stock price, up or down, sometimes by a lot.
facts.claim: Earnings reports can move a stock a lot, either way.

facts.quote: So, if you're considering buying or selling a stock, it may be a good idea to find out when the company plans to announce earnings.

walkthroughs.title: Four times a year
steps: A quarter ends, and over the next few weeks most public companies report. That's earnings season.
Most run on calendar quarters, so it kicks off early to mid January, April, July and October.
Hundreds of names report in a short window. It gets busy, and it can get volatile.
So check the date on everything you own or want. We don't buy in the 3 days before a report.

walkthroughs.title: Before the open or after the close
steps: Most companies report while the market's shut: before the 9:30 a.m. open or after the 4:00 p.m. close.
Report after the close and it can swing after hours. The regular session gets its say at the next open.
Report before the open, and that morning's open takes it. Either way, the close before is your last regular-session exit.
Get the time from the company's own release. Meta's said after the close on February 2, 2022.

walkthroughs.title: The implied move
steps: The options market puts a number on the report: a move, plus or minus. That's the implied move, or the expected move.
It's a size, not a direction. And it's not a cap. The real move can be bigger, smaller, or nothing at all.
Your stop can't catch a gap. So put that move in dollars on your whole position before you decide to hold.

questions.q: It's mid-April, and the names on your watchlist start reporting one after another. What's going on?
choices: Earnings season, a quarter ended
Quarter-end, the books are closing
Annual report season, once a year
Dividend season, most pay this month
questions.why: Earnings season. The quarter closed at the end of March, and now the reports roll in. That's the few weeks after each quarter ends, when most public companies put out their numbers. Most run on calendar quarters, so it kicks off in early to mid January, April, July and October. Four times a year, not once. Why you care: hundreds of names report in a short window, and the reactions can be fast and big. So when the season starts, I pull up the dates on everything I hold and everything I want to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Quarter ends, the reports roll in. That's earnings season, and it's when I check every date I own.

wrong.Quarter-end, the books are closing: The quarter already closed at the end of March. The reports come in the weeks after it.
wrong.Annual report season, once a year: Companies report every quarter, so the season comes four times a year.
wrong.Dividend season, most pay this month: Dividends have nothing to do with it. This is quarterly results coming out.

questions.simple: The few weeks after each quarter ends are earnings season, when most companies report, so check the dates on what you hold.

reasons: stable definition, several FINRA (Tier 1) facts agree

questions.q: You like a setup and plan to hold it a few weeks. Before you buy, which date do you pull up first?
choices: Its next earnings date
Its ex-dividend date
Its last earnings date
Its last stock split date
questions.why: The next earnings date. A report can move a stock a lot, up or down, and nobody knows which way ahead of time. If that date lands inside your hold, the report lands while you own it. That changes the whole trade. Whether you can buy at all, and whether you can hold through the report, both start from that date. You'll find it in the earnings list on the Calendar page in our app. Then confirm it on the company's own website before you get involved.
questions.lesson_line: Before I get involved, I check the date. Then I know if a report sits inside my hold.

wrong.Its ex-dividend date: That one's about the dividend. The earnings date is the one that can gap the stock.
wrong.Its last earnings date: That report is done. What matters is the next one, and whether it lands inside your hold.
wrong.Its last stock split date: That's history. The next report inside your hold is what can hurt you.

questions.simple: Look up the next earnings date first, because a report inside your hold can move the stock a lot either way.

reasons: the why points to our earnings rule (B22, the owner's rulebook) without stating it; q24 teaches it

questions.q: When do most companies release their earnings?
choices: Before the open or after the close
In the middle of the trading day
In the final hour of trading
Right at the 9:30 opening bell
questions.answer: Before the open or after the close
questions.why: Before the open or after the close. FINRA says companies usually release results then. Regular trading runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET, so the news lands while it is shut. Trading before 9:30 and after 4:00 is called extended hours, and the stock can still move sharply there. So the first thing to ask about any report is which side of the session it lands on.
questions.lesson_line: Most results land while regular trading is shut. Know which side of the session yours falls on.

wrong.In the middle of the trading day: FINRA says companies usually release results before the open or after the close, not mid-session.
wrong.In the final hour of trading: Results usually come after the close, not in the final hour.
wrong.Right at the 9:30 opening bell: Morning results usually come out before the open, while regular trading is still shut, not at the bell.

questions.simple: Most companies report before the open or after the close, so the news lands while regular trading is shut.

questions.q: Every public company reports in the same few weeks each quarter.
questions.why: False. Most companies use calendar quarters, so most report in the weeks after March, June, September and December end. Some don't. A retailer might end its quarter in January instead of December, to keep the holiday sales and returns together. It then reports on its own schedule. So never guess a name's report date from the season. Look it up for each stock you hold.
questions.lesson_line: Don't guess the date from the season. Look it up for each name you hold.
questions.simple: False, because some companies end their quarters in other months, so they report on their own schedule.

questions.q: Before a report, what does the implied move show?
choices: The move options are pricing in
Analysts' EPS growth estimate
Last quarter's actual move
The most the stock can move
questions.answer: The move options are pricing in
questions.why: The move options are pricing in. It's the size of move the options market expects from the report, up or down.
questions.lesson_line: The implied move is the options market's price on the report. Read it before you hold.

wrong.Analysts' EPS growth estimate: That's a fundamentals number from analysts. The implied move comes from option prices.
wrong.Last quarter's actual move: That's what already happened. The implied move is priced for this report.
wrong.The most the stock can move: It's no cap. The actual move can be bigger, smaller, or nothing at all.

questions.q: A name on your list just reported. The headline says it "beat." What does that tell you?
choices: Results topped the analysts' average
The stock price rose after the report
Results grew from a year earlier
It reported before the SEC deadline
questions.why: Results came in above the analysts' average. That average is the consensus, what the analysts who cover the stock expect. Come in above it and it's a beat. Fall short and it's a miss. That's all a beat tells you. It says nothing about where the stock goes next. A company can beat and still drop on a weak outlook. And the bar the market really trades against can be a whisper number, not the posted one. So I never buy a headline. I watch how the stock acts.
questions.lesson_line: A beat is the numbers against the estimate. How the stock reacts is a separate question.

wrong.The stock price rose after the report: That's the reaction, not the beat. Plenty of stocks beat and still drop.
wrong.Results grew from a year earlier: That's growth. A beat is results against what analysts expected for this quarter.
wrong.It reported before the SEC deadline: That's timing. A beat is about the numbers against the estimate.

questions.simple: A beat means results topped what analysts expected on average. It doesn't tell you the stock will go up.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A report out after the 4:00 p.m. close first trades in the regular session at the next ___.
questions.why: Open. Regular trading runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET. A report after the close can trade after hours first. The regular session first takes it at the next session's open, and gaps often show up there.
questions.lesson_line: A report after the close first hits the regular session at the next open.
questions.simple: The next open, because the regular session is shut after the 4:00 p.m. close until the next session starts.

questions.q: A stock trades 20% lower after hours on its report. That's where it will open tomorrow.
questions.why: False. After hours is a first read, not a forecast. The SEC warns that an extended-hours price may not match the next regular open. Meta's a good example. It traded at $249.90 after hours on Feb. 2, 2022, down 22.6%. It kept falling and closed the next day at $237.76. So don't build your plan on the after-hours print. Have your plan ready for the open, and let the regular session show you where it really wants to trade.
questions.lesson_line: After hours is a first guess. The open can be somewhere else.
questions.simple: False, because the price can keep moving after hours and overnight, so the open can be somewhere else.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (f19, SEC)

questions.q: JPMorgan set its Oct. 13, 2026 results for about 7:00 a.m. ET, and its call for 8:30 a.m. When does the regular session first trade them?
choices: At 9:30 a.m., the open that morning
At 7:00 a.m., the release
At 8:30 a.m., the call starts
At 9:30 a.m., the next day's open
questions.answer: At 9:30 a.m., the open that morning
questions.why: At 9:30 a.m., the open that morning. JPMorgan set its results for about 7:00 a.m. ET on Tuesday, Oct. 13, with its call at 8:30 a.m. Regular trading starts at 9:30 a.m. ET, so that same morning's open first takes the news. The stock can trade earlier in extended hours, but that is not the regular session.
questions.lesson_line: A report before the open hits that day's open. Your last regular-session exit is the close before.

wrong.At 7:00 a.m., the release: That's the release time. Regular trading starts at 9:30 a.m. ET; anything earlier is extended hours.
wrong.At 8:30 a.m., the call starts: That's the call time. The regular session still opens at 9:30 a.m. ET.
wrong.At 9:30 a.m., the next day's open: That's how a report after the close would play. This one came before the open.

questions.simple: At the open that morning, because the 7:00 release comes before regular trading starts at 9:30.

reasons: the release time rests on one cited fact (f27, JPMorgan's own notice)

questions.q: MSFT trades at $209.58 a few hours before its July 22, 2020 report. Options price a $9.48 move. How big is that, in percent?
questions.why: About 4.5%. Divide the dollar move by the price, then times 100. 9.48 divided by 209.58, times 100, is about 4.5%. That's the implied move, how big a move options are pricing on MSFT for the report. Up or down, they don't know which. You don't have to work it out yourself. Open the Calendar page in our app. The earnings list has an Impl. Move column, and you can sort by it to see the biggest priced moves. To do it by hand, take the at-the-money straddle in the nearest expiry. That's the call and the put at the strike closest to the price, here the 210. They were 4.75 and 5.15. Add them and you get 9.90. Then take off the 0.42 the 210 strike sits above the 209.58 price. That leaves 9.48. MSFT closed at $202.54 the next day, a drop inside that priced move. I check this number on anything I'm thinking of holding into a report.
questions.lesson_line: Turn the priced move into a percent. Our Calendar page shows it, or work it from the straddle.
questions.simple: About 4.5%, because 9.48 divided by 209.58 is about 4.5%. The Calendar page in our app shows it for you.

reasons: computed key (calc); inputs from one IBKR page, which refused a plain client (403) on 2026-11-12

wrong.22.1%: You flipped it and put the price over the move. The move goes on top.
wrong.9.5%: You read the $9.48 dollar move as a percent. On a $209.58 stock it's a lot less.
wrong.0.5%: A decimal slip. You moved the point one place too far.

questions.q: The implied move tells you how far the stock will move after the report.
questions.why: False. It's what options are pricing, not a promise. The actual move can be bigger, smaller, or close to nothing.
questions.lesson_line: Treat the implied move as the market's estimate. The real move can blow right past it.

questions.story: You hold two names into Tuesday's close. One reports Tuesday after the close. The other reports Wednesday before the open.
questions.q: When does each report first hit you in the regular session?
choices: Both at Wednesday's open
Tuesday's close, then Wednesday's open
Wednesday's open, then Thursday's open
Both at Tuesday's close
questions.why: Both hit at Wednesday's open. The first name reports once Tuesday's 4:00 p.m. close is done. So the first regular-session price on it is Wednesday's 9:30 a.m. open. The second reports Wednesday morning, before that same open. So both gaps land on you at once. That's the part people miss. The first one can trade after hours Tuesday night, but that's not the regular session. Tuesday's close is your last regular-session exit for both, so make the call on each one there.
questions.lesson_line: After the close or before the open, it all hits the next open. Make your call before the close.

wrong.Both at Tuesday's close: Neither one has reported yet at Tuesday's close.
wrong.Tuesday's close, then Wednesday's open: The first name reports after Tuesday's session ends, so Tuesday's session never trades it.
wrong.Wednesday's open, then Thursday's open: The second name reports before Wednesday's open, so Wednesday's open takes it.

questions.simple: Both hit at the same open, because one reports after the close and the other before the next open.

deeper.trap: Two reports, one exit. Hold both into Tuesday's close and two gaps can land at the same Wednesday open. If both gap down, both losses hit in the same session. Tuesday's close is your last regular-session chance to act on either.

reasons: timing logic from FINRA and SEC (Tier 1); stable

questions.story: You plan to buy a breakout and hold for a few weeks. The calendar shows a report in eight days, marked "Time Not Supplied".
questions.q: What's your move before you buy?
choices: Check the company's own website
Assume it reports after the close
Nothing, your stop has it covered
Trust the calendar date, it is official
questions.why: Go to the company's own website. "Time Not Supplied" means the calendar doesn't have the time yet. The date itself can be soft too, tentative or just guessed from past reports. The company settles both. Open its investor relations page and find the release that sets the date. Meta's, posted Jan. 4, 2022, said results after the market close on Feb. 2. JPMorgan's said about 7:00 a.m. ET on Oct. 13, 2026, before the open. The time tells you which open takes the gap, and when your last chance to sell is. With a report inside your hold, you need that plan before you buy, not after.
questions.lesson_line: The calendar gives you a lead. The company's website gives you the answer.

wrong.Assume it reports after the close: Plenty do, but not all. Guess wrong and the gap hits a whole session earlier than you planned.
wrong.Nothing, your stop has it covered: A stop is a trigger, not a price. It can't catch a gap.
wrong.Trust the calendar date, it is official: A calendar date can be tentative, or a guess from past reports. Only the company makes it official.

questions.simple: Check the company's own website, because the calendar date can be a guess and the time may be missing.

questions.q: You're holding 200 shares of a $40 stock into tonight's report. The implied move is ±9%. If it gaps down that much, what does it cost you?
questions.why: $720. Work it through. 200 shares at $40 is an $8,000 position. 9% of $8,000 is $720. That's the move options are pricing, either way. Now the part that matters. The implied move is no cap. The real gap can be bigger, and your stop can't sell above it. So before the close, look at that $720 and ask if you're fine losing it, or more. We only hold through a report when the trade is up 5R. Short of that, you're out before the number.
questions.lesson_line: Put the implied move in dollars on your position. That's the loss to plan for, and it can be bigger.
questions.simple: 200 shares at $40 is $8,000, and a 9% gap down takes $720. A real gap can be bigger.

wrong.$1,800: You took the 9% as $9 a share. It's 9% of the position.
wrong.$7,200: A decimal slip, one zero too many.
wrong.$8,000: That's the whole position. The gap takes 9% of it, not all of it.

questions.q: You buy at $36 with a stop at $34. Earnings gap it down and the stop fills at $32. How many times your planned loss did you lose?
questions.why: Twice. You planned to risk $2 a share, from $36 down to $34. The gap filled you at $32, double the loss you planned.
questions.lesson_line: A gap can turn your planned loss into a bigger one. Size for the gap, not just the stop.

questions.q: The morning after a report, the live implied move reads far smaller than last night. Why?
choices: The news is out, so volatility fell
The stock can't move much now
Analysts lowered their estimates
Fewer people trade the options
questions.answer: The news is out, so volatility fell
questions.why: The news is out, so volatility fell. In the weeks before a report, option volatility usually rises and makes options pricier. Once the news is out, most of the uncertainty is gone and options reprice fast. So the implied move shrinks. It does not mean the stock can't move. The options simply stopped pricing the report.
questions.lesson_line: Read the implied move before the report. After it, the number deflates.

wrong.The stock can't move much now: It can still move. The options simply stopped pricing the report.
wrong.Analysts lowered their estimates: Estimates don't drive this. The drop comes from volatility leaving the options.
wrong.Fewer people trade the options: The implied move is read from option prices, and they reprice fast once the news is out.

questions.simple: The report is over, so the options no longer price in its big unknown, and the implied move shrinks.

deeper.trap: Read the implied move before the report, not the morning after. Option volatility often collapses after the first reaction to earnings. So a reading taken after the news looks calm, even on a stock that just gapped.

questions.q: Your stock beat estimates four quarters in a row. That makes it safe to hold into the next report.
questions.why: False. Beating is normal, so a streak tells you less than it feels like. On FactSet's 5-year average, 78% of S&P 500 companies beat their EPS estimates. So four beats in a row doesn't make your stock special. What moves the price is the outlook, and how far the stock ran into the report. A company can beat and still drop on a weak outlook. A stock that ran hard into the report can meet the numbers and stall, with no new buyers left. And the downside is lopsided. Around the report, beats gained 0.9% on average and misses lost 3.1%. So the streak doesn't change anything. We hold through a report only when the trade is up 5R. Otherwise you're out before it.
questions.lesson_line: A beat streak is history, not a forecast. Into a report, I hold only when I'm up 5R.
questions.simple: False, because most companies beat, and a beat can still drop on a weak outlook. Past beats don't make a report safe.

deeper.trap: A beat streak feels like safety, but beating is the normal case: 78% of S&P 500 companies beat on FactSet's 5-year average. What moves the price is the outlook and the run into the report. FINRA notes a company may beat and give a weak outlook. A stock that rallied into its report may lack new buyers. And the miss hurts more than the beat pays: on that same average, beaters gained 0.9% and misses lost 3.1%.

questions.q: A company can beat the consensus estimate and still disappoint the market.
questions.why: True. The market's real bar can be a whisper number above the consensus. A beat with a dour outlook can drop too.
questions.lesson_line: Beating the posted estimate isn't the same as beating what the market wanted.

questions.q: FactSet's 5-year average: beats gained 0.9%, misses lost 3.1% around the report. How many times bigger is the miss?
questions.why: About 3.4 times. Measured from two days before to two days after the report, S&P 500 misses cost far more than beats paid.
questions.lesson_line: The market hits a miss harder than it pays a beat. Respect the downside into a report.

questions.story: You hold Meta (then ticker FB) with a sell stop at $300. It reports after the close on Feb. 2, 2022. After hours it trades at $249.90, down 22.6%.
questions.q: If it opens near there, where does your stop actually fill?
choices: Far below $300, at the market
At $300, the stop price you set
At the last close, before the news
Nowhere until $300 trades again
questions.why: Far below $300, at the market. Your stop price is a trigger, not a promise. Once the stock trades through it, the stop turns into a market order and takes whatever price is there. If Meta opens near $249.90, that's about where you sell, way under your $300. And it got worse. Meta closed that Thursday at $237.76, down 26%. A stop-limit would skip the bad fill, but it might never fill at all, and then you're still holding. That's why your stop distance isn't your risk into a report. The gap is.
questions.lesson_line: A stop can't sell above a gap. Into a report, the gap is your real risk.

wrong.At the last close, before the news: That price is gone. The report reset everything after the close.
wrong.Nowhere until $300 trades again: That's how a stop-limit acts, and it might never fill. A plain stop sells at the market.
wrong.At $300, the stop price you set: The $300 only triggers the order. The fill is whatever the market pays.

questions.simple: Far below $300, because a stop turns into a market order once it's hit, and the market is way lower.

deeper.trap: In a gap, the price jumps with no trading in between, so nothing trades at your stop price. The stop triggers and sells at the market, and the fill can land far below the stop. Into a report, the gap is the real risk, not the stop distance.

reasons: touches the owner's gap rule (B20) and real stop orders (D41); see owner_flags

questions.story: You hold a $20,000 position into tonight's report. Your stop is 4% below the price. The implied move is ±10%.
questions.q: If you hold, what loss do you plan for?
choices: About $2,000, and maybe more
About $800, plus a little slippage
None, the stop caps the loss
About $1,000, half of the ±10%
questions.why: About $2,000, and maybe more. 10% of $20,000 is $2,000. Your stop says $800, 4% of $20,000. But a gap that size jumps right over a 4% stop. The stop triggers and sells at the market, under its price. And the implied move is no cap, so the real gap can be bigger. That's how I measure risk into a report: by the implied move, not the stop. If $2,000 or more is too much to lose, don't hold it into the number. We only hold through a report when we're up 5R anyway.
questions.lesson_line: Into a report, I measure risk by the implied move, not my stop distance.

wrong.About $800, plus a little slippage: That's 4% of $20,000, your stop distance. A gap doesn't stop at your stop, and the fill can land far below it.
wrong.None, the stop caps the loss: A stop caps nothing in a gap. It triggers and sells at whatever the market pays.
wrong.About $1,000, half of the ±10%: The ± means 10% either way, not 10% split in two. A $10 move on a $100 stock spans $90 to $110.

questions.simple: Plan for $2,000 or more, because a 10% gap on $20,000 jumps right over a 4% stop.

deeper.trap: Your stop distance is not your risk into a report. A 4% stop on $20,000 says $800. A gap the size of the implied move, 10%, costs $2,000, and the stop cannot sell above the gap. With shares alone, the only sure way to cap that risk is to be out before the report.

questions.story: Your stock ran hard for weeks into its report. The numbers come in solid, right on expectations. It opens flat, then slips.
questions.q: What best explains the slip?
choices: Few new buyers were left after the run
The implied move capped the upside
It missed the consensus estimate
questions.answer: Few new buyers were left after the run
questions.why: Few new buyers were left after the run. FINRA notes a stock that rallied into its report and met expectations may lack new buyers to push it higher.
questions.lesson_line: A big run into a report raises the bar. Meeting expectations may not be enough.

wrong.The implied move capped the upside: The implied move is no cap. The real move can be bigger, smaller, or nothing at all.
wrong.It missed the consensus estimate: It came in right on expectations, so it didn't miss. The run before the report is the problem.

questions.story: You own a smaller social media stock. The group's biggest name reports after the close tonight. Yours reports later.
questions.q: Should tonight's report matter to you?
choices: Yes, it can move the whole group
No, only your own report can move it
Not unless you also own the big name
Yes, but a beat there can only help
questions.answer: Yes, it can move the whole group
questions.why: Yes, it can move the whole group. A big name's report doesn't stay in its own lane. Feb. 2, 2022 is the one to remember. Meta reported after the close, and Snap fell more than 18% after hours that night. The next day Snap lost 23%, on Meta's news, not its own. So check when the leaders in your group report, not just your own name. If the biggest stock in your group reports tonight, you're exposed to that gap too.
questions.lesson_line: Check the leaders' dates too. Their report can gap your stock.

wrong.No, only your own report can move it: Big names move their groups. Snap gapped on Meta's report.
wrong.Not unless you also own the big name: You don't have to own it to feel it. The group trades together.
wrong.Yes, but a beat there can only help: Not always. A company can beat and still fall on a weak outlook, and drag its group down with it.

questions.simple: Yes, because a big name's report can drag its whole group, the way Meta's did to Snap.

deeper.example: Meta reported after the close on Feb. 2, 2022, and fell 26% the next day. Pinterest, Snap and Twitter all slid after hours that night. The next day Snap lost 23% and Twitter dropped 5.6%. Check when the leaders in your group report, not just your own stock.

reasons: two Tier 2 publishers (CNBC, CBS) agree; historical, fixed numbers

questions.q: A breakout triggers today. The company reports a week from now. You can still buy it.
questions.why: True. We don't make new buys in the 3 days before a report. A week out is outside that, so the buy is fine. But the report is coming, so plan for it on the way in. We only hold through a report when the trade is up 5R, five times what you risked. So you've got about a week to get there. If it isn't up 5R by then, you sell before the report. Know that before you click buy.
questions.simple: True, because we only block new buys in the 3 days before a report, and a week out is further away.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys 3 days before a report. A week out, you can buy. Be up 5R or out by the report.

reasons: days versus sessions is an open owner question elsewhere; a week out is clear under either reading

questions.q: Earnings season starts well before the SEC's deadline for filing the required reports.
questions.why: True. Companies may put out their results before they file the required SEC forms, and most do. So the season gets going well before the filing deadline.
questions.simple: True, because most companies put out their results before they file the forms the SEC requires.
questions.lesson_line: Most results come out before the filing deadline. Don't wait for the filing to find the date.
